_comment: What a glyph-name component says about the glyph's font properties.
There is no general convention -- each family names its variant cuts its
own way -- so these are keyed by a regular expression matched against the
font name, and hold only what has actually been observed in that family.
Add a family by surveying it first:  gpm_names.py <font> --list
Components that are size or shape variants (.sm .dsp .var .s1 .dtls .x .l
.r .m .t) are deliberately absent: they are not font properties.
stix keeps an upright cut of the integrals beside the usual slanted one
in the same font (uni222B vs uni222B.up), which no codepoint distinguishes
and no comparison against another font can settle.
A 'base' rule substitutes the base character rather than a property, and
only where it already reads one of the keys.  .dtls is the dotless cut:
the codepoint at that position is the ordinary letter's (u1D55A decomposes
to 'i'), so only the name says the glyph has no dot.  Unicode has just two
dotless forms, plain and italic, so every other font falls back to the
plain one -- which gpm_to_lua reports rather than hides.

There is no 'selector' rule any more.  A size cut's sequence is MEASURED (gpm_ladder, from <font>.metrics.json) rather than read off the suffix: the measurement covers the plain cut too, which no suffix can name, and it knows the rung depends on the kind of character -- an n-ary operator's plain cut is its text cut and takes FE01, a delimiter's plain character takes none.  A hardcoded selector here was a second source for the same fact and drifted from it: .dsp said FE01 while the operator convention wants FE02.
